questions.question: What does the power set $\mathcal P(A)$ contain?
options: All elements that are not in $A$.

questions.question: Which two subsets are always included in $\mathcal P(A)$?
If a finite set has $n$ elements, how many elements does its power set have?
Why is $\varnothing\in\mathcal P(A)$ true for every set $A$?
options: Because the power set excludes nonempty subsets.
Because $\varnothing$ is always an element of $A$.

questions.question: What is the power set $\mathcal P(\varnothing)$?
options: It has exactly one element, namely $\varnothing$.

questions.question: If $A=\{a,b\}$, which is $\mathcal P(A)$?
If $A=\{1,2,3\}$, what is $|\mathcal P(A)|$?
For $A=\{1,2\}$, which object is an element of $\mathcal P(A)$?
For $A=\{1,2\}$, why is $1\notin\mathcal P(A)$?
options: Because $1$ is an element of $A$, not a subset of $A$.
Because $1$ is a subset of $A$, not an element.
Because power sets contain only numbers larger than $2$.
Because $\{1\}$ is not a subset of $A$.

questions.question: What is $\mathcal P(\{\varnothing\})$?
Why is the notation $2^A$ natural for a power set?
options: It means $A$ must be a set of numbers.
It means the power set contains exactly two subsets for every set.
For each element of $A$, a subset makes one of two choices: include it or exclude it.
It means every element of $A$ is multiplied by $2$.

questions.question: What does Cantor's theorem say about the size of $\mathcal P(A)$?
options: It always has the same cardinality as $A$.
It is smaller than $A$ whenever $A$ is infinite.
It has larger cardinality only when $A$ is finite.
It has strictly larger cardinality than $A$.

questions.question: Is $\mathcal P(A)$ usually a subset of $A$?
options: No. Its elements are subsets of $A$, not usually elements of $A$.
Yes. Every power set is contained in the original set.
Yes, but only when $A$ is finite.

questions.question: If $A$ is finite and $|\mathcal P(A)|=16$, what is $|A|$?
Which subset of $\{x,y,z\}$ has exactly two elements?
Which set has exactly one element?
Why does $A\in\mathcal P(A)$ hold?
options: Because the power set contains only proper subsets.
Because every set is an element of itself.
Because every set is a subset of itself.

questions.question: Cantor's theorem gives $|A|<|\mathcal P(A)|$ for every set $A$. Which conclusion does this rule out?
options: There is no bijection from $A$ onto $\mathcal P(A)$.
There is no subset of $\mathcal P(A)$.
There is no function from $A$ to $\mathcal P(A)$.
There is no injection from $A$ into $\mathcal P(A)$.

questions.question: Let $A=\{0,\{0\}\}$. Which list gives all elements of $\mathcal P(A)$?
If $A=\{a,b\}$, what is $|\mathcal P(\mathcal P(A))|$?
